query: Earlier studies of conventional metallic multilayers provide a general framework for deformation, but its conclusions may not transfer directly to high-entropy-alloy systems because compositional complexity, severe lattice distortion, and short-range order are associated with unusual deformation behavior. Preliminary evidence from FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy multilayers remains insufficient to establish what controls creep or when a given response dominates. Within the constraints of retaining a nanoscale multilayer coating and balancing strength with deformation tolerance, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading? State what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would expose it, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, boundary conditions, relevant prior support, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FCC/BCC high-entropy alloy multilayers, sustained loading at intermediate temperatures progressively activates plastic deformation because local lattice distortions and short‐range chemical clustering at the coherent FCC/BCC interfaces reduce the barrier for dislocation climb. This facilitates a gradual transfer of dislocations from the softer FCC layers into the stronger BCC layers via interface‐mediated stress relief.
generation.material_initial_state: A nanoscale multilayer coating composed of alternating FCC and BCC high-entropy alloy phases exhibiting coherent or semi-coherent interfaces with initial low defect densities and a characteristic degree of chemical short-range order.
generation.intervention: Subject the multilayer coating to sustained, constant stress (creep testing) at an intermediate temperature where thermally activated processes (dislocation climb) are operative but without inducing full recrystallization.
generation.conditions: Tests performed at moderate temperatures (e.g., several hundred °C depending on the alloy system) and applied stresses below the yield point for immediate flow, ensuring that the multilayer microstructure remains intact while capturing progressive plasticity.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent FCC/BCC interfaces whose local chemical short-range order and lattice distortions create regions of reduced climb barrier that mediate dislocation activation and transfer.
generation.mechanism: Dislocations initially nucleate in the relatively softer FCC layers under loading and accumulate at the FCC/BCC interfaces due to lattice mismatch and short-range ordering. Under sustained stress, these dislocations undergo stress-assisted climb—a process facilitated by local lattice distortions and compositional clustering—to bypass barriers and transfer into the stronger BCC layers. This results in a coordinated, progressive plastic deformation without compromising the nanoscale multilayer architecture.
generation.predicted_outcome: Creep or sustained loading experiments will reveal an initially low strain rate that gradually accelerates as dislocation climb and interface activity become dominant. Microscopy (e.g., TEM) should show dislocation pile-ups, jog formation, and local rearrangements at the FCC/BCC interfaces correlating with regions of chemical clustering or ordering, relative to an as-processed baseline multilayer with minimal interfacial defects.
generation.baseline: Multilayer coatings in the as-deposited state having coherent interfaces and uniform short-range order, showing limited plastic deformation when unloaded or under low-stress, short-term loading.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to prevail under intermediate temperatures and stresses that promote thermally activated dislocation climb but not at cryogenic temperatures (where climb is suppressed) or at very high temperatures where additional mechanisms (like dynamic recrystallization or grain boundary sliding) may intervene.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of dislocation climb versus slip (or even potential dynamic recrystallization at higher loads) and the sensitivity to variations in chemical short-range order remain to be fully established. Additionally, the role of potential competing deformation mechanisms in multilayers with even finer layer thickness is not yet certain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical FCC/BCC HEA multilayer specimens; one set is left in its as-deposited state while the other undergoes an annealing treatment to deliberately modify (reduce) the interfacial short-range order. Subject both sets to identical sustained creep loading at an intermediate temperature. Use high-resolution TEM and in situ diffraction methods to monitor dislocation structures and interface evolution during deformation.
measurements: Overall creep strain rate versus time/stress curves
TEM observation for dislocation pile-ups, jog formation, and evidence of interface-mediated dislocation climb
Assessment of any changes in local chemical ordering at the interfaces (e.g., via atom probe tomography or high-resolution EDS mapping)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments do not show a higher density of dislocation climb markers (e.g., jogs, interface disruption) in the as-deposited multilayers compared to the annealed ones, or if load-induced plastic deformation does not correlate with the predicted activation of climb at the FCC/BCC interfaces, then the hypothesis—that interfacial short-range order and lattice distortions govern the progressive plasticity through dislocation climb—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. The observed jog configurations are indicative of a dislocation climb process, and thus the stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion may be the operative creep mechanism of the present high-entropy alloy in LSR. Contrary to LSR, creep deformation in HSR exhibits abnormally high stress exponents of 8.9–14 and an average activation energy of 380 kJ mol −1 . Combined with the dislocation configurations in Figure 8 c and Figure 9 c, the same creep mechanism may also be considered rate-controlling. The unusually high stress exponents and activation energy in several traditional alloys have been frequently described using the power-law breakdown equation [ [43] , [44] , [45] , [46] ]. However, no deviation from the linear relationship on double-logarithmic curves of log ε ˙ ~ log σ were observed, and therefore, the power-law breakdown assumption may be inappropriate for the present alloy.
